name: Senegalese Thieboudienne
description: Thieboudienne, Senegal's national dish, depends on real technique from the very first step: the fish is cut with deep slits and stuffed with a real garlic-parsley-chili paste called the roof, not just seasoned on the surface. The rice then cooks directly in the fish-and-vegetable broth, absorbing everything, and is meant to form a light crust at the bottom of the pot, a genuine sign it's done right.

standing in for the roof's chili

ingredients_full.ingredient: Rice, white, long-grain, parboiled, enriched, dry

ingredients.note: tbsp, standing in for parsley, chopped, for the roof

steps_detailed: Mix the cilantro, half the garlic, and half the jalapeño into a coarse paste (the roof).
Cut deep diagonal slits into the fish and stuff the roof paste directly into the cuts.
Pan-fry the stuffed fish briefly, 3-4 minutes per side, then set aside.
Fry the onion and remaining garlic, add the tomato paste, cook 2 minutes, then add the diced tomatoes and 2 cups water and simmer 10 minutes.
Add the carrot and cabbage, and simmer 12-15 minutes until tender.
Stir in the rice and simmer 18-20 minutes, undisturbed toward the end, until tender and a light crust forms at the bottom of the pot.
Return the fish to warm through before serving.

name: Senegalese Yassa Poulet
description: Yassa, chicken marinated and slow-cooked in a mountain of caramelized onions and lemon, is one of Senegal's most beloved dishes, the onions cooked down until sweet being the whole point, not a garnish.
steps_detailed: Marinate the chicken in the lemon juice and garlic for at least 20 minutes, or up to overnight.
Brown the chicken, 6-7 minutes, then set aside.
Cook the onion in the remaining oil over medium-low heat, stirring often, 20-25 minutes, until deeply softened and sweet - this long cook is what makes yassa what it is.
Return the chicken to the pot with a splash of water and simmer 15 minutes more.
